title: Peony for the Soon Departed 3
content:
Two months later found them in Yunmeng.

With the catastrophic fall of the Qishan Wen Sect, the Nightless City—once the most dazzling, sleepless jewel of the cultivation world—vanished into smoke overnight, reduced to a hollow graveyard of rubble. A massive tide of cultivators, displaced and scrambling for new stomping grounds, splintered across the realm. Most of them poured straight into the Four Great Sects: Lanling, Yunmeng, Gusu, and Qinghe. Along Yunmeng’s main thoroughfares, people shoulder-to-shoulder thronged the streets. Highborn disciples and guest cultivators swaggered by with spiritual swords strapped to their waists, loudly dissecting the current geopolitical landscape with insufferable attitudes, brimming with self-importance.

All at once, the ambient chatter dropped to an uneasy hush. Heads turned in unison toward the far end of the avenue.

Drifting down the stone path was a young man in immaculate white, his cloud-patterned forehead ribbon fluttering gently in the breeze. A seven-stringed guqin was strapped across his back, a masterwork blade resting at his hip.

He was breathtakingly handsome, yet a suffocating aura of frost and snow seemed to trail his every step. Long before he drew near, cultivators instinctively bit their tongues, stepping aside to offer silent, reverent salutes. A few bold enough to possess some reputation took a cautious step forward, bowing low.

"Hanguang-jun."

Lan Wangji inclined his head in a microscopic, flawless nod, returning the courtesy with surgical precision before pressing on without breaking stride. The other cultivators, terrified of overstepping their bounds, quietly melted back into the crowd.

Right then, a girl draped in vibrant, multicolored silks came skipping toward him with a bright, beaming smile. She breezed past his shoulder, and with a sudden flick of her sleeve, hurled something straight at him.

Lan Wangji’s hand whipped up like striking lightning, catching the projectile clean out of the air. Opening his palm, he looked down to find a delicate, snow-white flower bud.

It was fresh and pristine, still beaded with morning dew. Before Lan Wangji could process the gesture, another lithe figure drifted into his path, pitching a tiny pale blue blossom straight at his chest. Her aim was off—it bounced harmlessly off his shoulder. Lan Wangji pinched the petals out of the air. When his cool gaze flicked up, the maiden let out a cheeky giggle, threw a sleeve over her blushing face, and bolted down the street without looking back.

A third time. A young girl with her hair tied in playful double buns came bounding over like a rabbit, clutching a slender sprig dotted with tiny crimson buds. She tossed the branch squarely against his sternum, spun on her heel, and took off sprinting.

Once, twice, three times. Before he knew it, Lan Wangji was left standing dead in the middle of the crowded avenue with an armful of vibrant, multicolored blossoms, utterly stone-faced. The cultivators in the street who recognized Hanguang-jun were desperately trying not to choke on their own laughter; they threw on grave, dignified expressions, though their eyes kept darting toward him like frantic moths. The common townsfolk who had no idea who he was had already started nudging each other and pointing.

Just as Lan Wangji lowered his eyes, lost in thought, a sudden, feathery weight brushed the crown of his hair. He reached up. A lush, pink peony in full, wanton bloom was perched neatly right against his temple.

From high above, a teasing, lilting voice floated down through the air: "Lan Zhan—ah, my mistake, Hanguang-jun. Fancy seeing you here!"

Lan Wangji tilted his chin toward the sky. Above him sat a grand open-air pavilion, its diaphanous silk curtains drifting lazily in the wind. A slender, black-clad figure was draped across the vermilion balustrade, leaning back on one elbow. Dangling from his loose fingertips was an exquisite black ceramic wine jar, its brilliant crimson tassel half-looped around his wrist and half-swinging in a lazy pendulum above the street.

The second they caught sight of Wei Wuxian’s face, the expressions on the surrounding disciples morphed into something fascinatingly sour. The entire world knew the Yiling Laozu and Hanguang-jun went together like oil and water. Even fighting side by side on the frontlines of the Sunshot Campaign, they’d thrown down in bitter screaming matches at every turn. Nobody had the faintest clue what circus was about to unfold, completely ditching their aristocratic manners to gawk at the pair with shameless intensity.

Lan Wangji didn't flick his sleeves and storm off in a huff as the crowd expected. He simply stared up at the balcony. "It's you."

"Guilty as charged!" Wei Wuxian beamed back. "Who else would pull something this childish? What brings you all the way out to Yunmeng? If you’re not in a rush, why not come on up for a drink?"

A flock of pretty young women crowded around him at the railing, leaning over the painted edge to chime in with a chorus of giggles: "Yes, Young Master, come up and have a cup!"

Those very girls were the ones who had just pelted him with blossoms. Who had put them up to the stunt was blindingly obvious.

Lan Wangji dropped his gaze, spun on his heel, and strode away.

Seeing that the bait hadn't taken, Wei Wuxian wasn't in the least bit surprised. He gave a quiet click of his tongue, rolled off the balustrade, tipped his head back, and took a deep, greedy swig straight from the jar.

A moment later, unhurried, measured footsteps echoed from the stairs.

Lan Wangji ascended the landing with immaculate posture, his pale hand parting the hanging curtain. The glass beads clattered together with a bright, rhythmic chime that sounded almost musical.

He dumped the mountain of blossoms that had struck him straight onto the low wooden table. "Your flowers."

Wei Wuxian propped his chin on his palm, slouching across the table. "Don't mention it! Consider them a gift—they’re all yours now."

"Why?"

"No reason," Wei Wuxian said with a grin. "Just wanted to see what kind of face you’d pull if someone ambushed you like that."

Lan Wangji’s tone was ice. "Childish."

"Of course it's childish! Why else would I go through the trouble of hauling you up here? ...Whoa, hey, don't walk out! You already climbed all those stairs—aren't you going to stay for a cup?"

"Alcohol is forbidden."

"I know it's banned in your house," Wei Wuxian wheedled. "But we’re in Yunmeng, not the Cloud Recesses! Knocking back a cup or two out here won't kill you."

The maidens instantly produced a fresh porcelain cup, poured it to the brim, and slid it right next to the heap of flowers. Lan Wangji made no move to sit, but he didn't turn to leave either.

Wei Wuxian pressed his advantage. "It's not every day you drop by Yunmeng—you really aren't going to sample our local vintage? Though I have to admit, as good as our stuff is, it still can't hold a candle to your Gusu's Emperor’s Smile. That stuff is true perfection. Next time I manage to swing by Gusu, I'm definitely going to stash eight or ten jars and drink myself under the table. Look at you, though—what is your deal? There's a perfectly good cushion right there, and you're insisting on standing like an iron pillar. Sit down, will you?"

The girls chimed in, fluttering around him: "Take a seat!" "Yes, sit with us!"

Lan Wangji’s pale eyes swept a frigid glance over the radiant, giggling maidens. His gaze drifted downward, locking onto the glossy black flute resting at Wei Wuxian’s waist, adorned with its crimson tassel. He seemed to lower his chin, carefully turning over his words.

Seeing the pause, Wei Wuxian’s brow ticked up. He already had a sinking feeling he knew exactly what lecture was coming.

Sure enough, Lan Wangji spoke, his voice measured and grave: "You should not spend your days in the company of the non-living."

The teasing smiles on the maidens' faces vanished into thin air.

A sudden draft billowed through the silk drapes, blotting out the sunlight and casting the terrace in shifting, gloomy shadows. In the dim light, the girls’ porcelain complexions looked alarmingly pale—drained of every drop of blood, tinting a ghastly, bruised green. Their dark pupils bored straight into Lan Wangji, fixed and unblinking, an eerie, suffocating chill bleeding into the warm tavern air.

Wei Wuxian raised a casual hand, gesturing for them to stand down. He shook his head, sighing, "Lan Zhan, the older you get, the more boring you become. You’re barely out of your youth—it's not like you’re pushing eighty! Why do you always have to copy your uncle, scolding people with that stiff, holier-than-thou routine?"

Lan Wangji turned, closing the distance between them by a single, deliberate step. "Wei Ying. Come back to Gusu with me."

Wei Wuxian went quiet. After a beat, he chuckled dryly. "Man... it’s been an eternity since I heard you say that. The Sunshot Campaign is over and done with; I honestly thought you’d finally given up on that crusade."

"During the hunt on Phoenix Mountain," Lan Wangji said, "did you not notice the warning signs?"

Wei Wuxian frowned. "What warning signs?"

"You lost control."

"You mean almost throwing hands with Jin Zixuan?" Wei Wuxian scoffed. "I think you’re confused. I alwayswant to beat the shit out of Jin Zixuan the second I lay eyes on him."

"And the words you spoke afterward."

"What words?" Wei Wuxian asked breezily. "I run my mouth all day, every day. You expect me to remember what I blabbed about two whole months ago?"

Lan Wangji held his gaze, seeing right through the flippant deflection. He drew in a slow, sharp breath. "Wei Ying."

His tone was stubborn, unyielding: "The demonic path harms the body, and it corrupts the soul."

Wei Wuxian pinched the bridge of his nose, feeling a migraine coming on. "Lan Zhan, come on... I’ve heard this sermon a hundred times already. Aren't you tired of repeating it? You say it ruins the body, but I'm standing right here in one piece. You say it warps the soul, but it's not like I’ve gone around butchering innocents like a rabid dog."

"It is not yet too late," Lan Wangji pressed. "If you wait until you are drowning in regret—"

Before the sentence could land, Wei Wuxian’s smile dropped completely. He pushed himself abruptly to his feet. "Lan Zhan!"

Behind him, a crimson, feral gleam sparked to life in the eyes of the silent maidens. Wei Wuxian murmured without looking back, "Hold your positions."

The girls dipped their heads and obediently drifted into the shadows, though their murderous glares remained pinned to Lan Wangji. Wei Wuxian turned back to him, his tone clipped and quiet: "Look. I don't believe for a second that I'm ever going to 'drown in regret.' But more importantly, I really don't appreciate people casually predicting my doom."

An agonizing silence stretched between them. Finally, Lan Wangji spoke: "I have overstepped."

"You're fine," Wei Wuxian said, leaning back. "Though it seems inviting you up here was a mistake on my part. My apologies for troubling you today."

Lan Wangji murmured, "You did not."

Wei Wuxian offered a thin, polite smile that didn't reach his eyes. "Is that so? Glad to hear it."

He tipped back the cup, draining the rest of his wine in one clean swallow. "Still, thanks anyway. I'll just take it as you looking out for me."

With an airy wave of his hand, he turned toward the stairs. "I won't keep Hanguang-jun from his business. Until next time."

By the time Wei Wuxian strolled back through the gates of Lotus Pier, Jiang Cheng was sitting in the courtyard polishing his spiritual sword. He flicked his eyes up. "Back?"

"Back."

Jiang Cheng sneered, "You look like absolute hell. Run into Jin Zixuan or something?"

"Worse than Jin Zixuan," Wei Wuxian sighed. "Take a guess."

"Give me a hint."

"Someone who wants to lock me in a cage."

Jiang Cheng’s brows pinched together. "Lan Wangji? What the hell is he doing in Yunmeng?"

"Search me," Wei Wuxian said, waving a hand. "Lurking around the market. Tracking someone down, probably. Ever since the war wrapped up, he hadn't brought that nonsense up once. Now he's right back on his soapbox."

Jiang Cheng scoffed, "And who told you to call out to him in the first place?"

Wei Wuxian blinked. "How did you know I was the one who called him over?"

"Do I even need to ask? Isn't it always you?!" Jiang Cheng rolled his eyes so hard they nearly stuck. "I don't get you at all. Every single time you two cross paths, you part ways on the verge of killing each other. So why do you tirelessly throw yourself at him just to get hated on?"

Wei Wuxian tilted his head, mulling it over. "Because I was bored?"

Jiang Cheng shot him a blistering look that screamed at least you know it, before turning his attention back to his steel. Wei Wuxian asked, "How many times a day do you need to polish that thing?"

"Three times," Jiang Cheng answered flatly. "Where's your blade? How long has it been since you touched it?"

Plucking a fresh pear from a wooden bowl on the table, Wei Wuxian took a loud, juicy bite. "Tossed it in my room. A wipe-down once a month is plenty."

Jiang Cheng scolded, "From now on, don't show up to major events like grand hunts or discussion conferences without your sword. You're handing everyone a free excuse to call you ill-bred and undisciplined on a silver platter."

"You know me," Wei Wuxian shrugged. "The more people try to force me to do something, the less I want to do it. If I don't feel like wearing a sword, who's going to stop me?"

Jiang Cheng threw him a venomous side-eye.

Wei Wuxian took another bite, continuing, "Besides, I have zero interest in getting roped into sparring matches with strangers. The moment my blade clears its scabbard, it demands blood. Unless someone's serving up a couple of bastards for me to butcher, they can leave me the hell alone. Leaving it behind solves the whole problem—peace and quiet."

Jiang Cheng’s tone turned dry. "You used to love showing off your sword forms in front of a crowd."

"I was a kid back then," Wei Wuxian said softly. "Nobody gets to stay a kid forever."

Jiang Cheng let out a short, hollow scoff. "Fine. Leave the sword behind, I don't care. But stop picking fights with Jin Zixuan. He's Jin Guangshan's only legitimate heir—he's the future head of the Lanling Jin Clan! When you trade blows with him, what am I supposed to do as clan leader? Jump in and jump him with you? Or punish you publicly?"

Wei Wuxian countered, "Doesn't he have Jin Guangyao now? Jin Guangyao is ten times easier on the eyes than that peacock."

Jiang Cheng finished wiping down the blade, inspecting the edge before sheathing Sandu with a sharp, metallic clack. "What good is looking pleasant? No matter how sharp or agreeable he is, he's just a glorified retainer running errands for his father. His ceiling is set in stone; he can't hold a candle to Jin Zixuan's bloodline."

Hearing the blatant deference in his tone, Wei Wuxian stared at him. "Jiang Cheng, give it to me straight: what are you playing at? You went out of your way to drag Shijie to the hunt last time... you don't actually want them to end up together, do you?"

Jiang Cheng replied evenly, "Why not?"

"Why not?!" Wei Wuxian’s voice spiked. "Did you completely wipe your memory of what he pulled at Langya?! And you're telling me why not?!"

"He probably regrets it."

"Who gives a damn about his regret?!" Wei Wuxian spat. "Just because an asshole realizes he was wrong means he gets an automatic pass? Look at his old man's wandering eye—mark my words, Jin Zixuan is going to turn out the exact same way, chasing skirts from one end of the map to the other. You want Shijie saddled with that? You could actually stomache that?!"

Jiang Cheng’s eyes darkened, his voice dropping lethal: "He wouldn't dare."

He paused, casting a pointed, heavy glance at Wei Wuxian. "Besides, whether we forgive him isn't up to you or me. A-Jie likes him. What else can we do?"

Wei Wuxian choked on his own breath, utterly robbed of words.

After an agonizing silence, he ground out through his teeth, "Out of everyone in the world... why does it have to be that prick?"

He tossed the pear core into the grass. "Where's Shijie?"

Jiang Cheng grunted, "Who knows? It's always the same three spots: the kitchen, her bedchambers, or the ancestral hall. Where else would she go?"

Leaving the Sword Testing Hall behind, Wei Wuxian checked the kitchens first. A small ceramic pot of soup was simmering gently over the low embers, but the room was empty. He swung by her chambers next—still empty. Finally, he padded toward the ancestral hall.

Sure enough, she was there.

Jiang Yanli was kneeling on a woven straw mat, softly murmuring under her breath as she gently dusted the ancestral tablets of her parents. Wei Wuxian poked his head through the lattice doorway. "Shijie? Gossiping with Uncle Jiang and Madam Yu again?"

Jiang Yanli looked up with a tender smile. "Since neither of you ever visit, someone has to keep them company."

Wei Wuxian slipped inside, dropping onto the mat beside her, grabbing a cloth to help wipe down the lacquered wood.

Jiang Yanli tilted her head, eyeing him fondly. "A-Xian, why are you staring at me like that? Do you have something to tell me?"

Wei Wuxian grinned. "Nothing at all! I just came in to roll around."

To prove his point, he threw himself sideways, literally rolling across the polished floorboards like a clumsy puppy.

Jiang Yanli chuckled, "And just how old is our Xianxian today?"

Wei Wuxian beamed up from the floor. "Three years old!"

Seeing her laugh, he finally pushed himself back into a seated cross-legged position. He hesitated for a brief beat before murmuring, "Shijie... can I ask you something?"

"Go ahead."

Wei Wuxian asked, "Why does a person fall in love with someone else? I mean... that kind of love."

Jiang Yanli blinked, caught off guard. "Why the sudden curiosity? Do you like someone? What kind of girl is she?"

"No, definitely not!" Wei Wuxian protested immediately. "I’m never falling for anyone. Or at least, never too deeply. Isn't that just strapping a plow around your own neck and handing someone else the reins?"

Jiang Yanli smiled warmly. "Three years old might be giving you too much credit. Let's go with one."

"Hey, I'm three! And three-year-old Xianxian is starving! What are we going to do about it?!"

Jiang Yanli chuckled, "There's soup in the kitchen, go have some. Though, I wonder if three-year-old Xianxian can even reach the stove?"

"If I can't reach, Shijie can just pick me up—"

Before the nonsense could finish spilling from his lips, Jiang Cheng strode into the hall, sneering, "Still spewing garbage, I see! This Sect Leader already ladled a bowl and left it on the veranda. Crawl out there, thank me on your knees, and choke down your soup."

Wei Wuxian scrambled outside, only to march right back in. "Jiang Cheng, what the hell? Where are the pork ribs?!"

Jiang Cheng shrugged without a shred of remorse. "Ate 'em. Only lotus root left. Take it or leave it."

Wei Wuxian jabbed an elbow straight into his ribs. "Spit them back out!"

"Fine, I will! Let's see if you've got the guts to swallow them!"

Seeing the two instantly revert to squabbling toddlers, Jiang Yanli raised her hands in exasperated surrender. "Alright, honestly, how old are the two of you to be brawling over a few ribs? I'll just go brew another pot..."

Wei Wuxian adored Jiang Yanli’s lotus root and pork rib soup above all else.

It wasn't just because the broth was sweet, rich, and comforting—it was because he could never forget the very first time he’d tasted it.

Back then, Jiang Fengmian had only just scooped a feral, half-starved Wei Wuxian off the streets of Yiling. The moment the scrawny boy crossed the threshold of Lotus Pier, he’d caught sight of a proud little young master sprinting around the drill yard with a pack of tiny puppies tumbling at his heels. Terrified out of his wits, Wei Wuxian had shrieked, buried his face in Jiang Fengmian's neck, and wailed until his voice was raw—clinging to the sect leader's robes for an entire day, refusing to touch the ground. The very next morning, all of Jiang Cheng's beloved puppies were quietly packed up and given away.

Jiang Cheng had wept until his eyes swelled shut. Even with Jiang Fengmian coaxing him with gentle words, telling him they needed to "be good brothers," the boy refused to speak a single word to Wei Wuxian. After several days, Jiang Cheng’s frosty demeanor finally showed signs of thawing. Hoping to strike while the iron was hot, Jiang Fengmian decreed that Wei Wuxian would share Jiang Cheng's bedchambers, praying the proximity would bridge the divide.

Jiang Cheng had been on the verge of reluctantly nodding along. But the fatal mistake occurred when Jiang Fengmian, swept up in a burst of paternal joy, scooped Wei Wuxian up into his arms and hoisted the boy onto his shoulders. Jiang Cheng had stood frozen, staring in absolute, hollow shock. Madam Yu had let out a venomous scoff on the spot, flicking her sleeves and storming out. If both parents hadn't been rushing out on urgent clan business, a screaming match would have erupted right then and there.

That very night, Jiang Cheng barred the door from the inside, leaving Wei Wuxian stranded out in the cold.

Wei Wuxian tapped timidly on the wooden lattice. "Shidi... Shidi, let me in. I need to sleep."

Inside, Jiang Cheng pressed his small back against the heavy wood, shouting through tears, "Who's your shidi?! Give me back Feifei! Give me back Jasmine! Give me back Xiao-Ai!"

Feifei, Jasmine, and Xiao-Ai were the names of his puppies. Knowing full well they were gone because of him, Wei Wuxian whispered miserably, "I'm sorry... But... but I'm really, really scared of them..."

In Jiang Cheng's entire childhood, his father had picked him up fewer than five times—and every single instance was a memory precious enough to sustain his happiness for months. A bitter, suffocating knot of resentment twisted in his chest, screaming why him, why him, why him? Catching sight of the extra set of bedding laid out across his private floor, that frantic jealousy boiled over. He scooped up Wei Wuxian’s quilt and straw mat.

Outside, Wei Wuxian was waiting anxiously when the door suddenly swung open. Before he could smile, an avalanche of cloth and woven straw slammed into his chest, knocking him flat onto his rear. The door slammed shut with a concussive bang.

Jiang Cheng screamed from the other side, "Go sleep somewhere else! This is my room! You want to steal my room too?!"

Back then, Wei Wuxian hadn't understood Jiang Cheng’s fury in the slightest. "I'm not stealing it," he muttered, baffled. "Uncle Jiang told me to stay here."

Hearing him mention his father only made it feel like a deliberate, cruel brag. Jiang Cheng’s eyes burned scarlet as he howled, "Get lost! If I see your face again, I’m setting a whole pack of dogs on you!"

Hearing the word dogs, pure, blinding panic gripped Wei Wuxian's heart. Clasping his trembling hands, he scrambled to his feet. "I'm going, I'm going! Please don't call the dogs!"

Dragging the bundle of bedding behind him, he sprinted blindly down the covered veranda. He had barely set foot in Lotus Pier; he didn't dare explore, spending his days meekly confined to the few corners Jiang Fengmian designated. He didn't know the layout, didn't recognize the rooms, and certainly didn't dare knock on a stranger's door for fear of waking a master. After wandering in circles, he found a windless corner of the wooden walkway, spread his straw mat, and curled up beneath the quilt.

Yet the harder he tried to sleep, the louder Jiang Cheng's threat echoed in his skull. Every gust of wind, every rustle of the lotus leaves sounded like a hungry pack of feral hounds stalking toward him in the dark. Unable to bear the terror, he jumped up, rolled his mat, scooped his quilt, and bolted straight out the gates of Lotus Pier.

Panting in the brisk night air, he sprinted until his lungs burned. Spotting an ancient, sprawling tree, he scrambled up the trunk without a second thought, wrapping his limbs tightly around the highest bough he could reach. Only perched high in the leaves did his racing pulse finally slow.

He clung to that bark for what felt like hours. Then, drifting through the dark, came a soft, lilting voice calling his name.

The calls drew nearer, and soon, a young girl in pale robes stepped beneath the canopy, carrying a paper lantern.

Recognizing Jiang Cheng's older sister, Wei Wuxian held his breath, praying the leaves would swallow him whole.

Jiang Yanli halted, looking up. "Is that you, A-Xian? What are you doing all the way up there?"

Wei Wuxian stayed dead silent.

Lifting the lantern higher, she chuckled softly, "I can see you. You dropped your shoe."

Wei Wuxian peeked down at his bare left foot, gasping, "My shoe!"

"Come down," Jiang Yanli coaxed. "Let's go home."

Wei Wuxian choked out, "I... I can't. There are dogs."

"A-Cheng was just teasing you," she murmured gently. "There are no dogs. There's nowhere to sit up there; your arms are going to give out, and you'll fall."

No matter how she coaxed, Wei Wuxian refused to budge, hugging the bark for dear life. Terrified he’d slip, Jiang Yanli set her lantern by the roots, stretched her small arms wide, and stood directly beneath the bough, refusing to step away. After an incense stick of stubborn standoff, Wei Wuxian’s scrawny arms finally turned to jelly. His grip slipped, and he plummeted.

Jiang Yanli lunged forward to break his fall, but the impact sent them both tumbling across the dirt. Wei Wuxian rolled into the grass, clutching his shin and wailing, "My leg's broken!"

Jiang Yanli checked him over, soothing him, "It isn't broken, and it isn't fractured. Does it hurt badly? It's alright, don't move. I'll carry you back."

Still traumatized, Wei Wuxian whimpered, "Are... are the dogs coming...?"

"No," she promised firmly. "If any dogs come, I'll chase them away for you."

She picked up the lost shoe from the roots. "Why did it fall off? Does it not fit?"

Biting back tears, Wei Wuxian blurted out, "It fits! It fits fine!"

In truth, it was far too large. But it was the very first pair of brand-new shoes Jiang Fengmian had ever bought him; Wei Wuxian had been too terrified of being a burden to complain. Jiang Yanli slipped the shoe back onto his foot, gently pinching the empty leather at the toe. "It is a little big. I'll take it in for you when we get back."

Hearing that, Wei Wuxian felt an overwhelming wave of guilt, shrinking inward.

When you live under another man's roof, your greatest terror is becoming an inconvenience.

Jiang Yanli hoisted the boy onto her back, her small boots taking unsteady, deliberate steps down the path. "A-Xian," she whispered, "no matter what A-Cheng said to you tonight, don't hold it against him. He has a prickly temper. He usually plays all by himself, and those puppies were his absolute favorites; having Father give them away broke his heart. But deep down, he's thrilled to have someone around to play with. When you vanished for so long, he panicked, terrified something had happened to you, and rushed to shake me awake so I could find you."

Jiang Yanli was only two or three years his senior—barely twelve or thirteen at the time. A child herself, yet she naturally carried the steady, soothing warmth of a tiny matriarch, endlessly comforting him. Her frame was frail, her strength modest; she wobbled every few paces, pausing to hitch Wei Wuxian higher on her hips so he wouldn't slide down. Yet nestled against her back, Wei Wuxian felt an unprecedented, absolute sense of safety—far safer than perched upon Jiang Fengmian's shoulders.

Suddenly, a faint, ragged sobbing drifted on the night breeze.

Jiang Yanli flinched, whispering, "What was that? Did you hear it?"

Wei Wuxian pointed toward a dark slope. "Over there! It's coming from that ditch!"

They crept to the edge of the pit, carefully peering down. Curled at the bottom was a small, dusty silhouette. Looking up, twin tracks of tears had washed clean streaks through the grime on his cheeks as he choked out a wet rasp: "...Jiejie!"

Jiang Yanli let out a massive breath of relief. "A-Cheng, didn't I tell you to wake the disciples and search together?"

Jiang Cheng just shook his head, miserable. After his sister had slipped out, he’d sat in his dark room, consumed by gnawing guilt and dread until he couldn't take it anymore, running out into the night to track them down himself. In his frantic rush, he’d forgotten a lantern, caught his foot on a root, tumbled headfirst into the ravine, and cracked his forehead open.

Jiang Yanli hauled her younger brother out of the pit, pressing a clean handkerchief against the bleeding gash on his brow. Jiang Cheng slumped into a pathetic heap, dark eyes sneaking guilty, fleeting glances at Wei Wuxian.

Jiang Yanli asked softly, "Don't you have something you want to say to A-Xian?"

Pressing the linen tight to his temple, Jiang Cheng mumbled into his collar: "...Sorry."

"Will you help carry A-Xian's bedding back inside later?"

Sniffling, Jiang Cheng muttered, "I already brought it back."

With both boys limping and battered, walking the remaining distance was out of the question. Jiang Yanli had no choice but to carry one on her back while cradling the other against her chest. With Wei Wuxian and Jiang Cheng wrapping their arms around her neck like sticky burrs, she managed barely three paces before panting for air, laughing breathlessly, "What am I supposed to do with the two of you?"

Tears still clinging to their lashes, both boys tightened their grip around her neck in collective, guilty stubbornness.

In the end, she had dragged them back to Lotus Pier one agonizing step at a time. She’d quietly woken the clan physician, offering endless bows and apologies as the doctor dressed their wounds, before quietly seeing him off.

Jiang Cheng had stared at Wei Wuxian’s wrapped ankle, looking terrified. If the retainers found out about this and ran their mouths to his father, Jiang Fengmian would learn that he’d thrown Wei Wuxian out into the cold and crippled his leg—and he’d hate him even more. That was the sole reason Jiang Cheng had sprinted out alone instead of raising the alarm.

Seeing his terror, Wei Wuxian had offered an easy way out: "Don't worry, I won't breathe a word to Uncle Jiang. I'll just say I got an urge to climb trees in the middle of the night and slipped."

Hearing that, Jiang Cheng’s breath hitched in sheer relief. He swore right then and there: "Don't worry either! From now on, whenever there are dogs, I'll chase every single one of them away for you!"

Seeing the boys finally make peace, Jiang Yanli beamed. "Now that's how brothers should act."

After an exhausting night of tears and scrambling, their stomachs were roaring. Jiang Yanli slipped into the kitchens, standing on her tiptoes to stir the pots, warming up two generous bowls of lotus root and pork rib soup.

That fragrant warmth had nestled itself deep within his heart, lingering untouched by time.

Crouching in the quiet courtyard, Wei Wuxian set the empty porcelain bowl onto the flagstones. He stared up at the scattered, sparkling stars of the night sky, a faint smile touching his lips.

Running into Lan Wangji on the streets of Yunmeng today had dredged up a flood of memories from their youth back at the Cloud Recesses.

Calling out to him on a whim, Wei Wuxian had secretly wanted to steer the conversation back toward those simpler days. But Lan Wangji’s sharp warning had served as a stark reminder: nothing was the same anymore. The past was dead and buried.

Yet whenever he returned to Lotus Pier, whenever he was standing beside Jiang Cheng and Jiang Yanli, he could indulge in the fragile, beautiful illusion that nothing had ever changed.

A sudden impulse struck him: he wanted to find that old tree he’d climbed all those years ago.

Pushing himself up, he strolled toward the front gates. Disciples patrolling the walkways bowed and saluted with deep, formal respect. They were all unfamiliar faces. The playful, monkey-like martial brothers who refused to walk in a straight line, the cheeky servants who would wink and dodge formal courtesies—every single one of them was gone.

Crossing the drill grounds and stepping past the grand wooden threshold of Lotus Pier, the broad, bustling docks opened up before him. Day or night, street vendors always lined the water. The intoxicating aroma of sizzling street pastries hit the night breeze, and Wei Wuxian drifted toward the stalls with a grin. "Smells incredible tonight!"

The vendor laughed, "Young Master Wei, care for one? This one’s on the house, no need to tab it."

Wei Wuxian chuckled, "I'll take one, but put it on my tab as usual."

Squatting beside the frying cart was a filthy, disheveled figure. Before Wei Wuxian had walked up, the person had been shivering violently, clutching their knees against the cold, hollowed out by pure exhaustion.

Hearing Wei Wuxian speak, the figure’s head snapped up.

Wei Wuxian’s eyes went wide. "You?!"
